candidateRows: Group appearances reported by Paul and Luke provide historical grounds for concluding that Jesus was alive after his death.
This supplies the principal affirmative route from reported postmortem appearances to the physical resurrection asserted by the motion.
Trent frames resurrection as the sequence of life, death, and renewed life, grounding the final step in reported individual and group encounters.
Well-attested Marian apparitions raise the probability of Jesus's resurrection because such events fit Christian theology better if the resurrection occurred.
The argument broadens the affirmative cumulative case and directly incorporates rival or later miracle claims into a resurrection-supporting explanatory framework.
Trent treats some later supernatural reports as genuine and argues that resurrection provides a unified explanation for both early testimony and subsequent Christian phenomena.
Christian apparition reports do little to establish resurrection because comparable experiences occur elsewhere and the sources are unclear about whether Jesus's risen body was physical.
This challenges both the claimed distinctiveness of Christian experiences and the physical-resurrection interpretation required by the motion.
Trent's claim that Christian apparitions and group encounters support a physically risen Jesus.
Alex distinguishes occurrence from evidential force, arguing that Christian experiences are not unique and that Pauline and gospel descriptions pull in different directions on physicality.
Mormon witness and transfiguration traditions are at least comparable to early Christian appearance testimony, exposing how little can be verified about Paul's five-hundred-person report.
The comparison attacks the affirmative inference standard by presenting rival testimony with persistence, persecution, multiple witnesses, and in some respects closer sourcing.
Trent's reliance on group appearances, early testimony, and the rarity of collective resurrection encounters.
Alex compares Christian testimony with Mormon witnesses and a reported mass transfiguration, then stresses the anonymity, indirect transmission, and limited checkability of Paul's report.
Paul taught embodied resurrection rather than disembodied survival, and the physical features of Jesus's appearances distinguish them from acknowledged visions.
This defends the physical character of the alleged resurrection and answers the contention that Paul supplies only visionary or spiritually ambiguous testimony.
Alex's claim that Paul is unclear about physical resurrection and personally experienced only a vision.
Trent appeals to Paul's Pharisaic background and writings on transformed bodies, interprets spiritual language as orientation, and contrasts ordinary visions with bodily encounters.
Christian evaluation need not dismiss all later or non-Christian miracles, because genuine wonders outside Christianity can occur without validating a competing religion.
This supplies a consistency principle meant to preserve Christian miracle reasoning against the charge that rival claims are excluded by special pleading.
Alex's charge that Christian evidential standards privilege resurrection while discounting analogous non-Christian miracle claims.
Trent invokes Catholic openness to continuing miracles, allows divine action among non-Christians, and separates occurrence of a wonder from endorsement of its surrounding theology.
Mormon miracle and witness claims are materially weaker analogues because natural incentives, prior expectations, source discrepancies, and contrary historical evidence reduce their credibility.
This is the affirmative's principal attempt to defeat the rival-miracle comparison on evidential differences rather than merely rejecting non-Christian testimony categorically.
Alex's analogy between Mormon witnesses, persecution, transfiguration reports, and early Christian resurrection testimony.
Trent offers natural explanations for the transfiguration and plates, contrasts witness expectations and incentives, distinguishes Joseph Smith's risks, and cites countervailing historical claims.
The alleged expectation and financial-interest differences between Mormon and Christian witnesses are unstable because Jesus predicted resurrection and Mary Magdalene supported his ministry.
This directly contests two factual disanalogies on which Trent relies to prevent Mormon testimony from undermining the Christian appearance argument.
Trent's claim that Mormon witnesses were specially primed and financially invested unlike Jesus's disciples.
Alex argues that resurrection expectations were not absent from Jesus's circle and draws a parallel between Martin Harris's backing and Mary Magdalene's support and witness role.
Persecution and movement growth do not distinguish early Christianity from Mormonism, while the historical basis for claiming that apostles accepted death for resurrection belief is sparse.
This challenges the martyrdom and costly-commitment route by arguing that a rival movement endured comparable danger and expansion without validating its supernatural claims.
Trent's claim that Joseph Smith's conduct and incentives make Mormon costly commitment disanalogous to Jesus and the apostles.
Alex disputes treating armed resistance as decisive, questions evidence that apostles died for their faith, and compares Christian fear, Mormon persecution, and early growth rates.
Early Mormon growth under persecution parallels early Christian growth, so danger following a leader's death does not uniquely support the resurrection testimony.
The comparison challenges whether persecution, growth, and willingness to accept danger discriminate Christianity from a prominent rival miracle movement.
The earlier claim that danger after Jesus's execution supports the courage and credibility of his followers.
O'Connor argues that Joseph Smith's followers likewise faced violence after their leader's death and that Mormonism achieved a comparable early expansion rate.
Paul is unclear about a physical resurrection, while later Gospel appearance narratives become more elaborate and theological rather than supplying secure eyewitness history.
This directly disputes the historical basis for inferring a physical resurrection from Paul and the Gospel appearance narratives.
Trent Horn's earlier interpretation of Paul's language and the Gospel traditions as testimony to a physical risen body.

O'Connor contrasts Paul's ambiguous terminology with increasingly detailed later narratives, then uses the wounds and recognition stories to characterize important appearances as theological mythology.
The transfiguration and Matthew's mountain appearance contain signs of visionary experience that may illuminate the original character of resurrection appearances.
The argument offers a concrete visionary model for interpreting resurrection experiences instead of treating them as encounters with an ordinary physical body.
The earlier contention that the post-resurrection encounters and related bodily language describe physical historical appearances.
O'Connor links the transfiguration's sleep-adjacent setting, sudden figures, mountain setting, and subsequent doubt to a visionary interpretation of resurrection traditions.
The transfiguration can be physical and historical, and the canonical accounts are sober enough to differ materially from conspicuous later mythmaking.
This counters the visionary reading and defends a historical-literary distinction between canonical testimony and later legendary amplification.
O'Connor's claim that the transfiguration is visionary and resembles the underlying form of resurrection appearances.
Horn invokes traditions of bodily assumption for Moses and Elijah, Peter's practical reaction, and the exaggerated Gospel of Peter as a contrast with canonical restraint.
Apologetic purposes do not make a narrative false, and Matthew's dispute over a stolen body may preserve evidence that Jesus's body was genuinely missing.
The argument converts an alleged apologetic feature of Matthew into support for the empty tomb, a principal historical route to the resurrection conclusion.
The challenge that apologetic features and developing narrative details indicate defensive invention or mythmaking in the canonical Gospels.
Horn accepts that Matthew contains apologetic material but argues that the reported Christian-Jewish dispute presupposes a missing body requiring competing explanations.
Paul's bodily terminology denotes corporeal form, and the retained wounds identify the risen Jesus as the same embodied person who was crucified.
This directly supports the physical-resurrection component of the motion through Pauline language and continuity between the crucified and risen Jesus.
O'Connor's argument that Paul's references to a body remain ambiguous and do not establish a physically resurrected Jesus.
Horn appeals to Paul's consistent bodily vocabulary and interprets the crucifixion wounds as signs of triumph and personal bodily identity rather than narrative inconsistency.
Luke is historically reliable and close to Paul, while Paul's encounter was comparable to apostolic appearances and the bounded appearance tradition resists a hallucination hypothesis.
The move defends the sources for group and Pauline appearances and argues that their limited distribution is unlike uncontrolled visionary enthusiasm.
O'Connor's contention that Paul supplies only a private visionary experience and that the other appearance accounts lack eyewitness security.
Horn uses Luke's incidental historical accuracy and companionship with Paul, Paul's comparison with apostolic encounters, and the cessation of appearances to support a bounded historical event.
Apostolic suffering matters as evidence of sincere testimony by people positioned to know, and Christianity has additional explanatory features absent from the Mormon parallel.
The argument clarifies the intended evidential role of persecution and distinguishes informed apostolic sincerity from generic willingness to suffer for inherited beliefs.
O'Connor's comparison of persecuted early Christians with persecuted Mormons and his challenge to the evidential value of apostolic martyrdom.
Horn rejects the crude inference from dying for belief, focuses on informed witnesses risking death, cites evidence for several martyrdoms, and highlights Paul's conversion from opposition.
Early martyrdom sources are less decisive than claimed, canonical Matthew shares alleged legendary features, and Paul's comparison can support visionary rather than physical appearances.
The response challenges three major supports for the resurrection case: martyrdom evidence, canonical restraint, and the physical interpretation of Pauline appearances.
Horn's claims that early sources establish apostolic martyrdom, canonical accounts differ from mythmaking, and Paul corroborates physical appearances.
O'Connor questions what Clement establishes, notes reliance on apocryphal tradition, compares Matthew's guards and angel with later embellishment, and reverses Horn's inference from Paul.
Apostolic danger establishes sincerity rather than resurrection by itself, and apocryphal traditions must be sifted individually instead of rejected or equated with canonical accounts wholesale.
This preserves the limited martyrdom inference and supplies a historiographical answer to the attempted parity between canonical and apocryphal narrative material.
O'Connor's objections that martyrdom sources do not securely prove violent deaths and that canonical accounts exhibit the same mythmaking features as apocrypha.
Horn limits the suffering argument to witness sincerity, cites multiple early indications concerning Peter, and argues that exaggerated apocryphal motifs require case-specific evaluation.
The canonical tomb narratives display historically credible restraint, and their women witnesses and imperfect guard story are unlikely apologetic inventions.
This supplies a major historical-authenticity route for the empty tomb by contrasting canonical narrative features with conspicuous legendary embellishment.
O'Connor's contention that increasingly spectacular tomb traditions reveal apologetic development and weaken their historical credibility.
Horn distinguishes the restrained canonical accounts from the Gospel of Peter, defends the possible historicity of the guards, and treats women as first witnesses as an authenticity indicator.
Women discovering the tomb is narratively expected rather than an embarrassment criterion, while their immediate recourse to men and conflicting sequences weaken the apologetic inference.
This directly contests a prominent historical argument for the empty tomb and offers narrative function and inter-Gospel tension as rival explanations.
Horn's argument that choosing socially disfavored women as the first tomb witnesses strongly indicates that the account was not invented.
O'Connor argues that the women alone followed the burial and knew its location, that men soon verify their report, and that Mary's reactions and appearance chronology create tensions.
Appeals to a sufficiently clever inventor risk becoming unfalsifiable, while the women's conduct and the disciples' verification are also what the historical event would predict.
The move rebuts the proposed narrative explanation and articulates Horn's methodological test that evidence should be compared with expectations under actual occurrence.
O'Connor's claim that an ancient author could deliberately create realistic details and that women were narratively required because they knew the burial site.

Horn warns that clever-invention explanations can neutralize evidence regardless of its form, defends Joseph's knowledge and burial plausibility, and argues the reported reactions fit a real discovery.
Jesus' death and the rapid bodily-resurrection proclamation converge on an event best explained by resurrection without the compression and added assumptions required by alternatives.
This states the overarching abductive case for the motion, connecting agreed facts and early proclamation to the resurrection as a unified explanation.
O'Connor's broader skeptical treatment of the tomb narratives as explicable through literary construction, uncertainty, or non-resurrection scenarios.
Horn frames the inquiry as approaching Easter from the secure death of Jesus and the early bodily-resurrection proclamation, then compares the explanatory unity of resurrection with alternatives.
Evidence for Jesus before crucifixion is substantially stronger than evidence for postmortem appearances because the latter lacks independent extra-Christian corroboration.
This challenges parity between ordinary historical existence and resurrection evidence while specifying the missing corroboration that would materially strengthen the extraordinary claim.
Horn's claim that the evidential means for establishing Jesus alive after death are comparable to those establishing him alive before death.

O'Connor presents escalating historical thresholds, accepts existence and crucifixion, remains less certain about burial, and argues that independently attested appearance claims would be powerful but are absent.
The resurrection explains the conversions of prior unbelievers and persecutors and the transformation of frightened apostles into bold proclaimers.
The claimed transformations of James, Paul, and the apostles form an independent explanatory route from early behavior to a genuine resurrection encounter.
O'Connor's argument that post-resurrection appearances lack the independent corroboration that makes Jesus' pre-crucifixion existence historically secure.
Horn concedes that Gospel and Pauline evidence suffices for existence, then argues that denying resurrection makes several prominent conversions and apostolic courage harder to explain.
Persecution and martyrdom do not establish eyewitness knowledge of a bodily resurrection because the clearest early cases concern visionary experiences or unspecified beliefs.
This undercuts the martyrdom argument by separating sincerity from eyewitness access and by challenging whether the persecuted figures died for a witnessed physical event.
Horn's appeal to Paul, James, and persecuted apostles as people whose conversion and costly proclamation are best explained by the bodily resurrection.
O'Connor separates Paul's persecution from apostolic eyewitness claims, characterizes Paul and Stephen as vision cases, and stresses uncertainty about what Peter or James saw and why they suffered.
Acts can provide historically useful persecution testimony through Luke's companionship and reliability even without firsthand narration, while authorship claims should be weighed non-dogmatically.
The exchange bears on whether the sources supporting apostolic persecution and testimony are sufficiently connected and reliable to support the resurrection case.
O'Connor's insistence that Acts is not firsthand and that generalized Christian persecution cannot establish what particular apostles witnessed or died affirming.

Horn invokes Acts and non-Christian persecution evidence, defends Luke as a companion and historian, and accepts some uncertainty about Johannine authorship as part of calibrated historical reasoning.
An empty tomb, if there was one, is plausibly explained by temporary emergency burial followed by relocation or theft, neither of which requires resurrection.
This offers a detailed naturalistic rival explanation for one of the debate's key facts and argues that the data fit both resurrection and non-resurrection histories.
Horn's contention that the resurrection uniquely explains the historical data more naturally than skeptical alternatives and that the tomb evidence supports bodily rising.

O'Connor questions the burial setting, reads John as describing a nearby provisional tomb before Sabbath, surveys relocation and grave-theft possibilities, and treats them as more probable than resurrection.
Non-resurrection is only an umbrella for multiple specific hypotheses whose conjunction reduces probability, and grave robbery poorly fits the retained burial goods and known practices.
This defends resurrection's comparative explanatory force and directly attacks the probability and evidential fit of the principal naturalistic alternative just proposed.
O'Connor's proposal that emergency relocation or theft can explain the empty tomb more plausibly than resurrection and that non-resurrection fits the same data.

Horn argues that skeptical alternatives must be individually specified and often combined, then contends that thieves sought valuables and necromantic removal practices do not match taking the whole body while leaving goods.
Roman release of a crucified body for proper tomb burial was historically possible and has relevant precedent.
The move supports the historical plausibility of Jesus receiving a known tomb, a necessary foundation for the empty-tomb branch of the resurrection case.
The skeptical position that Roman crucifixion practice made release of Jesus' body for honorable tomb burial implausible.
During an exchange about grave robbery and burial practice, Horn invokes archaeological precedent to defend Roman authorization of a proper burial.
The Gospels' compassionate portrayal of Pilate is historically doubtful because Pilate was a ruthless ruler unlikely to care about Jesus.
This challenges a proposed motive for Pilate to release Jesus' body, weakening one supporting route to the narrated tomb burial.
Horn's suggestion that Pilate's political circumstances, guilt, or his wife's concern could explain granting Jesus a proper burial.
After burial is deemed institutionally possible, the discussion turns to whether the particular characterization and motives attributed to Pilate are credible.
Pilate's conflicts with Jewish authorities show that he sometimes accommodated political pressure, making release of the body historically fitting.
The response preserves the plausibility of Pilate granting a burial request despite his harsh character, supporting the tomb-burial premise.
O'Connor's contention that a ruthless and uncompassionate Pilate would have had no credible motive to accommodate Jesus' burial.
Horn distinguishes personal compassion from political calculation and points to Pilate's need to manage disputes with local Jewish authorities.
Mormon witness parallels do not neutralize the apostolic testimony because their defections and contradictory divine claims differ materially from the apostles' conduct.
It answers a major rival-miracle comparison intended to show that sincere or persistent testimony can support mutually incompatible religious claims.
The skeptical comparison between resurrection testimony and Mormon golden-plate witnesses as similarly sincere but unreliable religious testimony.
The exchange tests whether Mormon witnesses undermine an inference from apostolic sincerity; Horn argues that later repudiations and contradictions make the cases disanalogous.
Even a personal visionary experience could support belief, but the historical record does not provide comparably direct access to Jesus' physical resurrection.
The move clarifies that skepticism does not categorically exclude revelation while identifying the historical-access gap central to rejecting the resurrection inference.
The pro-resurrection case that reported apostolic and Pauline appearances supply adequate grounds for present historical belief.
Asked what evidence could convince him, O'Connor says a Damascus-like experience might matter personally but highlights uncertainty about its physical content.
Paul's reported experience was not purely private or mental because his traveling companions also perceived an external manifestation.
This supports the claim that the Pauline appearance had intersubjective features, resisting reduction to an isolated hallucination or private vision.
O'Connor's treatment of a Damascus-type encounter as potentially visionary and therefore insufficient to establish a physical resurrection.
Horn answers uncertainty about private perception by arguing that companions' awareness of light or another phenomenon gives the event external corroboration.
Visionary appearances need not be false, but their possible truth does not by itself establish that Jesus appeared in a physically resurrected body.
The distinction concedes genuine religious experience while blocking the inference from sincere appearances to the specific bodily-resurrection conclusion.
Horn's argument that externally noticed features of Paul's encounter move it beyond a merely subjective vision toward resurrection evidence.
O'Connor allows that visions can be veridical and applies that possibility to disciple traditions without treating visionary truth as bodily encounter.
A strong resurrection case would require firsthand bodily-appearance testimony plus evidence of persecution specifically for that belief, which the surviving record lacks.
This directly states why the available testimony and martyrdom evidence are insufficient to make faith in the bodily resurrection historically warranted.
The affirmative appeal to apostolic appearances, testimony, and willingness to suffer as sufficient historical support for bodily resurrection.
O'Connor says direct bodily testimony and belief-specific martyrdom would be formidable, but characterizes the evidence as visionary firsthand material or ambiguous secondhand reports.
The unprecedented early proclamation of bodily resurrection, sincere individual and group experiences, Paul's conversion, and a checkable tomb are best explained cumulatively by resurrection.
This is the affirmative's culminating explanatory case, combining the distinctive proclamation with sincerity, corroborated experiences, conversion, and the empty tomb.
O'Connor's conclusion that the sources are too indirect and ambiguous to justify belief in Jesus' bodily resurrection.
Horn argues that ordinary postmortem belief would not produce the historically unusual bodily claim and presents several mutually reinforcing facts as demanding explanation.
Better-documented later Christian miracle reports make universal dismissal of supernatural claims less probable and should weaken strict naturalism.
The move broadens the cumulative case by challenging the prior probability barrier that would otherwise exclude resurrection regardless of historical testimony.
The skeptical demand for stronger firsthand evidence and the naturalistic presumption that reported supernatural events are uniformly false.
Horn cites later reports with journalistic, photographic, and claimed physical corroboration, then urges comparison between universal falsehood and at least one genuine miracle.
